newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Monsengwo - a master conciliator.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Monsengwo - a master conciliator.

text.p: Roman Catholic Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo has more than once gone out on a limb to defuse crisis in his native Zaire.
He now faces his greatest challenge to date.

With Laurent Kabila's rebels demanding the immediate resignation of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and threatening to take the capital Kinshasa by force, many people are looking to him to save the city from a bloodbath.
Mobutu supporters in parliament, who once denounced him as an opponent and feared him as a competitor, voted on Saturday to give him back his old job as parliamentary speaker.

If he agrees, Monsengwo would become constitutional successor to Mobutu. As such, some say, he could become a possible key to a political settlement of Zaire's civil war that could avert a battle for the teeming capital of five million.
But Kabila's rebels, who were last reported 200 km (125 miles) from the city, have other thoughts.
They demand that Mobutu hand over power immediately to them and threaten to attack the capital if Monsengwo accepts.
Monsengwo, 57, crossed the Zaire River to Kinshasa from Congo on Monday to cheers from onlookers.
He had been out of public view since his 1995 defeat at the hands of an unnatural political alliance of Mobutu's supporters and followers of the president's fiercest opponent, Etienne Tshisekedi.

Even before his dismissal the music-loving Monsengwo had said he was tired of politics and needed to spend more time on pastoral work at his equatorial diocese in the eastern riverside city of Kisangani.

More than half Zaire's estimated 40 million people are Roman Catholics and in many remote corners of the sprawling state it is the Church which provides schools, hospitals, communications and even banks.

Monsengwo sprang to prominence in 1991, when he was elected head of a ground-breaking national constitutional conference, despite the efforts of pro-Mobutu supporters who accused him of opposition bias.
Only a short while earlier, the transition to democracy, announced by Mobutu in 1990 had collapsed into chaos as army-led looters ransacked Kinshasa and other major towns.

"What was at stake in this election was for the people to find someone who could help our people to reconcile themselves without exception, in a spirit of national unity, brotherhood and concord," Monsengwo said after being picked.
He won enormous respect as someone who was more swayed by rational argument than hot temper.

With a sharply analytical mind and an occasional schoolmasterly hand, Monsengwo managed to negotiate a path between supporters of Mobutu, including the army, and opposition radicals demanding political rights.

When more riots erupted in 1993 and economic depression and ethnic violence took hold of Zaire, Monsengwo again managed to bring the two sides together under one roof in a new transitional parliament, at least some of the time.
But the compromise he allowed in 1994, when Kengo wa Dondo was elected priem minister instead of Tshisekedi, cost him the support of the opposition radicals and eventually his job.
Radical opponents dubbed him "Judas" and "The Antichrist" for allowing the election of centrist Kengo.

Accused by Mobutu's supporters of being in league with the opposition, and the opposition of being a stooge of the president, Monsengwo was removed in a vote by the alliance of Mobutu's supporters and radical opponents in July 1995.
Monsengwo's supporters said Mobutu had managed to remove the one man whose following he really feared at elections -- even though the archbishop never expressed any indication he would stand.
Born in October 1939 Monsengwo was a quick and able student and was ordained in 1963. Throughout the 1970s he lectured in theology at the university of Kinshasa.
In 1981 Monsengwo became Archbishop of Kisangani and three years later was elected president of the Zairean Episcopalean Conference.
